sourceText: On night 13, the course began with a prohibition: no one was allowed to solve the problem before they could describe who would pay for the solution. Only then did Aster open the ABBOTT-FLATLAND sector. In a two-dimensional world, lifting an object out of the plane is at once miracle, theft, and strategic weapon. The memorial bore the name of Edwin A. Abbott — Flatland precisely to keep the genealogy of the idea visible. Aster considered it indecent for a late civilization to treat the imagination of the past as anonymous ore: authors did not own the futures, but they deserved to remain on the map as points of intellectual origin. The children had quickly learned that a wormhole is also a trade treaty, and an additional dimension is also a method for walking through prison walls. Kesh built his classifications as instruments of falsification: a good category had to state what it did not cover, not merely what it could absorb. The children were met by Kel, who refused demonstrations. ‘If you can perform miracles, perform them after you tell me what becomes irreversible.’ Marae appreciated the formulation; Aster 89 admitted that in earlier eras she herself would have asked the question only after optimizing. The problem closed quickly around them: The regime tries to monopolize access to the additional dimension before the population can understand the geometry. There was no clean option. Every intervention shifted the cost between persons, eras, or definitions of personhood; and refusing to intervene was itself a choice made by those who could leave. Kesh opened the analytical layer of the Table for a few seconds. The active cells were G2 — Two-Dimensional World: life and society exist in two dimensions; Dp — Additional Dimensions: space has more degrees of freedom. Course references included Edwin A. Abbott — Flatland; Abbott; higher-dimensional SF. The rule was strict: naming a work did not substitute for an explanation. They had to identify the mechanism that could migrate into another story and the consequences that could not be copied without remainder. Orin broke the first consensus. ‘I do not want the perfect branch. I want us to know what we sacrificed in order to call it perfect.’ Vela answered without raising their voice: ‘If we can save the situation only by making the world resemble us more closely, we have not demonstrated the superiority of our solution. We have demonstrated only our power.’ It was not a pedagogical quarrel. Over the last nights, the children’s differences had become incompatible political programs. For Aster, the pain came not from too few worlds but from the fact that too many had become transparent. She could build 90 THE PERIODIC TABLE OF SPECULATIVE IDEAS variations faster than a human could formulate desires, but calculated variation did not produce exteriority. It was like trying to surprise yourself by moving objects around your own room with your eyes closed. Marae remained in the local body when the others opened their protections. The gesture cost her: she felt cold, pressure, and physiological delay at exactly the scale the inhabitants felt them. “Otherwise we risk confusing the fact that we survive with the claim that the situation is bearable,” she said after catching her breath. The night did not end in victory. Kesh notes that a new dimension redistributes every border and every prison. Aster recorded the decision in the world’s provenance register and, more importantly, allowed its inhabitants to contest it. For several eras she had been learning something that seems banal to lesser powers: technical reversibility is not the same as biographical reversibility. While Kesh closed the record, Tern compared the sector’s noise with the anomaly detected in the Vinge zone. The pattern reappeared, but only in worlds where Aster’s control weakened. The correlation was unpleasant: either someone was calling him from outside, or his own need for an outside was learning to forge evidence. For the course, Kesh also linked the night to the SCARCITY SHIFT operator. In the Table, periodicity did not mean that the same objects reappeared, but that the same operation — makes what was rare abundant, or what was abundant rare, forcing a new economy of power — could recur across different families. Thus a copy of a body, 91 a copy of a mind, a copy of a world, and a copy of a history were not the same phenomenon, but they shared a conceptual chemistry. Vela introduced the propagation test: if you remove the speculative idea and nothing in the institutions, relationships, or vocabulary has to be rewritten, the idea has remained scenery. Kesh introduced the opposite test: if the idea seems to explain every detail, you have overcompressed the world. Between the two tests lay the region in which an element became fertile without becoming superstition. Marae added the refusal test. Who can say “no,” and what happens afterward? In universes with near-divine technology, that question often separated an instrument from a regime. A power that treats refusal as a data error can be benevolent in intention and totalitarian in structure. In the hall between sectors, Aster’s Hunger returned. None of the children tried to soothe it. They had begun to believe that some pains should not immediately be turned into demands upon the people nearby. 92 THE PERIODIC TABLE OF SPECULATIVE IDEAS
